historical_timeline.summary: Born in the Senegambia region of West Africa.
Arrives in Boston aboard the slave ship Phillis; bought by the Wheatley family; described as a frail child.
First known poem published in the Newport Mercury; renown follows with the Whitefield elegy of 1770.
Boston proposals for her volume of poems fail; publication is arranged in London.
Sails for London, partly for her health, to see her book through the press.
Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral is published in London; she returns to Boston.
Writes that she has her freedom, and that she has a cold and has had asthma since her return.
Marries John Peters; years of poverty follow.
Dies in poverty in Boston, aged about 31; her children did not survive.

claims.statement: In 1761 the child arrived in Boston aboard the slave ship Phillis (on 11 July, by one scholarly chronology) and was bought by the Boston merchant John Wheatley and his wife Susanna (or Susannah), in whose household she was enslaved as a domestic servant and companion. She was named Phillis after the ship and Wheatley after the family. The family judged her to be about seven because she was shedding her front teeth.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern social history: she was brought to Boston as a young child by traffickers and lived in the household that held her.

source_links.locator: 11 July: The approx. 7-year-old Senegambian child arrives in the Boston harbor aboard the slave ship Phillis. She is purchased by either Susannah Wheatley or her husband, John ... They name the Senegambian child, Phillis after the ship that brings her

In the month of August 1761, in want of a domestic, Susanna Wheatley, wife of prominent Boston tailor John Wheatley, purchased a slender, frail female child ... about seven years old ... from the circumstances of shedding her front teeth
Phillis became the domestic servant and companion of Mrs. Susannah Wheatley ... The first name Phillis was derived from the ship that brought her to North America

claims.statement: When she was bought in 1761 she was described as a slender, frail child, "evidently suffering from a change of climate"; the slave ship's captain is said to have sold her cheaply because he believed she was dying. One reference work describes her as "the frail, asthmatic child" and says she remained small and delicate.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented frailty and early label of asthma to which the modern presenting problem is linked. The description of her as asthmatic as a child rests on one reference work; no source describes her symptoms, triggers or treatment in childhood.

claims.statement: In the Wheatley household she was taught to read and write and within about sixteen months could read the Bible; she went on to read Greek and Latin classics and British literature. Her first known poem was published in the Newport Mercury in December 1767, and her elegy on the evangelist George Whitefield, published in 1770, brought her wide renown.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern social history: a widely read, published poet.

claims.statement: Proposals to publish a volume of her poems in Boston in 1772 found too few subscribers, and the volume was instead prepared for publication in London with the support of Selina Hastings, Countess of Huntingdon.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern concern with publishing her book and the planned journey.

claims.statement: In May 1773 she sailed for London with Nathaniel Wheatley, the family's son. The Massachusetts Historical Society says the voyage was "partly to regain her fragile health, but more importantly to shepherd her book of poetry through to publication"; another biography says she left "suffering from a chronic asthma condition."
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only, after the true-frame index date. The modern episode plans a sea journey for the same two reasons. (One biography misdates the departure to 1771; the Boston newspaper notice and the chronology give May 1773.)

claims.statement: She was freed soon after her return. On 18 October 1773 she wrote to David Wooster: "Since my return to America my Master, has at the desire of my friends in England given me my freedom," adding that whatever she earned from her book was now hers. One biography dates the manumission to some three months before Susanna Wheatley's death on 3 March 1774.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only, after the true-frame index date; her own letter is preferred to the later dating. The last visit of the modern episode reflects her new freedom.

The couple lived in poverty in Wilmington and Boston during and after the Revolutionary War; she worked as a maid or charwoman while continuing to write, and a proposal in 1779 for a second volume of her poems found too few subscribers.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Confirm asthma in a 19-year-old Black woman, born in West Africa, who has been called frail and asthmatic since childhood but never tested: spirometry with bronchodilator response read with race-neutral equations, FeNO and blood eosinophils, with tuberculosis excluded. Then treat on GINA 2025 track 1 (as-needed low-dose budesonide-formoterol, stepping to maintenance-and-reliever therapy after an exacerbation), write an action plan, address her triggers (cold air, cooking and fireplace smoke, colds), prepare her for a long sea journey and a summer away from her clinic, vaccinate, screen for depression and anxiety, and counsel on contraception and pregnancy planning with asthma (budesonide preferred, controller continued in pregnancy). Her social history at the true-frame index date is enslavement: the modern episode renders it truthfully as domestic servitude, and the clinic practises trauma-informed, patient-centred care in which she alone consents, decides and receives her information.

hpi.narrative: Miss Wheatley returns five weeks after the sick visit for asthma with a cold, when she stepped up to budesonide-formoterol as maintenance and reliever. The nurse telephoned her two days later and she was improving; she did not come for the review booked within a week, because she was very busy after her return. She never needed the standby prednisone. Her cold cleared within ten days; she now takes one inhalation twice daily and needs an extra one about once a week, and has not woken at night for three weeks. Her peak flow is 370 to 390 L/min. The screening tests from her preventive visit were negative for HIV, hepatitis C and hepatitis B surface antigen, and she has no immunity to hepatitis B. She has news she wanted to share: she now holds her own papers and her freedom, and whatever she earns from her book is her own. For now she still lives in the same house.

consultant_note.history: Miss Wheatley, 19, is seen at the request of Dr. Hartley-Okonkwo for three months of winter wheeze, cough and breathlessness, on a background of a weak chest since childhood that was called asthma but never tested. Symptoms come on three or four days a week, with waking about twice a month, and are brought on by cold wind, kitchen and fireplace smoke, and colds. She has never smoked, has never had an inhaler, and has never needed emergency care for her breathing. She may travel by sea in the spring. She was seen alone and gave her own consent
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Hartley-Okonkwo's intake note and results: chest X-ray clear; blood eosinophils 0.38; interferon-gamma release assay negative; urine pregnancy test negative; Asthma Control Test 15. This morning, in our laboratory, with GLI Global race-neutral equations: FEV1 2.24 L (83 percent predicted) before and 2.57 L after albuterol 400 mcg (+330 mL, +15 percent); FEV1/FVC 0.72 before, below the lower limit of normal of 0.75, and 0.80 after; FeNO 38 ppb. Total IgE 165 IU/mL; specific IgE positive to house dust mite and negative to cat and mold

exam.finding: Slight and composed, speaking in full sentences; oxygen saturation 98 percent
Nasal mucosa normal; no polyps
Faint expiratory wheeze on forced expiration; no crackles; no clubbing
Regular rhythm; no murmur

assessment.display: Asthma, confirmed, mild persistent, with type 2 inflammation
assessment.assessment: Question 1: this is asthma. The FEV1/FVC below the lower limit of normal that rises to normal after albuterol, with a 330 mL (15 percent) rise in FEV1, shows variable, reversible airflow obstruction. Tuberculosis infection is excluded by the negative interferon-gamma release assay, and the clear chest X-ray argues against bronchiectasis or scarring; nothing in her history suggests inducible laryngeal obstruction. Question 2: with race-neutral GLI Global equations her FEV1 is 83 percent of predicted; older race-based equations would have set a lower predicted value and could have made her obstruction look like none at all. Question 4: FeNO 38 ppb, blood eosinophils of 0.38 and sensitization to house dust mite show type 2 inflammation, which responds well to inhaled corticosteroid. Her most important triggers are cold air, smoke from cooking and fires, and colds; dust mite matters in the bedroom

recommendations: Question 3: GINA track 1, step 2: budesonide-formoterol 160/4.5 mcg, one inhalation as needed for symptoms and before going out in the cold, up to 12 a day; no albuterol-only reliever. This halves the risk of severe exacerbations compared with albuterol alone and suits her symptoms on several days a week

Teach technique with a spacer and check it at every visit; review six weeks after starting and within a week of any exacerbation; step up to maintenance and reliever (step 3) if control is not reached or after an exacerbation, and step back down when she is well
A written action plan with peak flow zones, and a two-week diary to set her personal best
Triggers: ventilate the kitchen and avoid fireplace smoke; a scarf over the mouth in cold wind; mite-proof bedding covers

Question 5: for the journey, two inhalers and the spacer, zones set from her personal best, a standby five-day course of prednisone with clear start rules for when care is far away, treatment for seasickness, an aired cabin away from smoke, and a printed summary; spirometry and FeNO again after her return

Question 6: well-controlled asthma is safe in pregnancy and uncontrolled asthma is the main risk; budesonide is the inhaled steroid with the most reassuring pregnancy data, and her treatment should continue, not stop, if she becomes pregnant; plan a review before and during any pregnancy
Vaccines: influenza and COVID-19 each season, and PCV20 once, as an adult with asthma

provenance_review.notes: She died in 1784; the recent-death rule does not apply. Claims rest on two Massachusetts Historical Society items (her letter of 30 October 1773 with transcription, and the October 2023 feature quoting her letter to David Wooster), the Poetry Foundation and National Women's History Museum biographies, the Society of Early Americanists chronology and one Gale reference work. Her childhood asthma rests on one reference work (D, probable); her own letter documents asthma after her return in 1773. The brief's statement that she died soon after childbirth is not supported by the fetched sources and is left out.
